newsitem.title: CROATIA: Opposition, media slam blackout on ailing Tudjman.
newsitem.headline: Opposition, media slam blackout on ailing Tudjman.

text.p: Croatia's opposition parties and independent newspapers accused state-controlled media on Monday of reverting to communist methods by shrouding President Franjo Tudjman's illness in secrecy.
Tudjman, 74, was flown to Walter Reed hospital in Washington last Wednesday.

After Western media broke the news on Friday Zagreb state television, which is controlled by Tudjman's ruling HDZ party, tersely acknowledged he was in hospital in a brief statement at the end of its prime time news.

"We are in a situation which is rather reminiscent of communism, when the health condition of the president is treated as top secret," Vlado Gotovac, head of the main opposition Social Liberal party, told Reuters. "That is ridiculous becaue it only causes concern among people.
"Our state media still have communist habits -- they will keep saying the president is feeling well as long as they can, because they think it is politically correct," he said.
Ever since Croatia broke away from federal Yugoslavia in 1991, the television has given detailed coverage of the president's daily agenda.

This time, rather than denying American reports that Tudjman had cancer, it said he had digestion problems caused by a stomach ulcer. On Saturday it reported he was feeling well and had scheduled a tennis match upon his return to Zagreb.
Zdravko Tomac of the former communist party said state media should "deny (Western reports) if they are not true".
"The worst thing is to hold something back from the people because then they start believing in rumours," he told Reuters.
Asked on Monday about the progress of Tudjman's recovery, his spokesman Tihomir Vinkovic told Reuters he had "no comment to make".
Authroities forced Nacional, a leading independent weekly, to scrap an early Monday edition because it contained abundant reports on Tudjman's condition.
Editor-in-chief Ivo Pukanic told Reuters he had sent a reporter to Washington and gathered enough information for Monday's edition.
"The president's illness is a matter of major importance for the fate of the country and we thought the only way to put an end to speculation is to publish the truth on time," he said.
On Saturday, however, hours before going to print, he was telephoned by "highest state officials" and ordered to scrap the edition.
"One senior official said we had to postpone the printing for Tuesday," Pukanic said. "He told me "24 hours means a lot in politics'."
Another independent weekly, Globus, said it was preparing a 15-page report on Tudjman for its next edition, but editor Davor Butkovic admitted "the official sources had been closed".

"It is exceptionally irresponsible from state bodies in charge of informing the public to have failed to do so on this occasion," said Zlatko Tomcic, president of another major opposition party, the HSS (Croatian Peasant Party).
